newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Anbari sees Iraq oil sale delay to early August.
newsitem.headline: Anbari sees Iraq oil sale delay to early August.

text.p: Key Iraqi envoy Abdul Amir al-Anbari, who negotiated December's U.N. food-for-oil deal, reiterated on Monday that he expected bureaucratic delays to push resumed Iraqi oil exports back until early August.

Anbari also said Iraq was easily capable, in the truncated period available, of meeting its permitted $2 billion target for oil sales in a second phase of exports which must be complete by early December.
"It would take about a month for the new resolution to be implemented, including the oil sales," said the diplomat in an interview with Reuters on a stopover in Geneva.
"I think end of July, beginning of August, the new resolution would come into force ... If all goes well, we'd resume sales in early August," he said.

Anbari was taking a slightly more pessimistic view of the prospects for Iraq's return to the world market than Oil Minister Amir Rasheed. The minister said last week he saw exports starting immediately a new aid distribution plan was in place, by about the end of this week.
Oil traders also said they were sceptical shipments would begin quite as quickly as Rasheed had hoped.
Anbari is Iraqi president Saddam Hussein's diplomatic trouble-shooter and is now based in Paris as ambassador to UNESCO, U.N. Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation.

He said he was now "a sort of roving ambassador" for Iraq and that it was likely he might be involved in negotiations with the United Nations again ahead of December when the oil-for-food deal comes up for renewal.
Iraq sees the oil sale deal as a temporary arrangement and is pressing for sanctions to be lifted entirely later in the year.

Oil markets have been waiting for word on the resumption of Iraq's oil sales since it got Security Council permission for new shipments from June 8 after approval of the second round of the oil-for-food deal, a humanitarian exception to sanctions slapped on Baghdad for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
The accord allows Baghdad to sell up to $2 billion of oil over 180 days to purchase food and medicine for civilians.
"People are yawning and reading newspapers at our oil exporting organisations. We'd very much like to become an important player on oil markets again," said Anbari.

"If all goes well, and if everyone is as enthusiastic as Iraq, it (oil sales) could even resume within two weeks. But from my experience, I know how slow and bureaucratic some of the organs of the U.N. Secretariat in New York is," added the envoy who has served in New York and London as Iraq's ambassador.
Anbari said Washington could further delay sales. "It all depends on the United States. They can shelve our distribution plan or oil pricing formula."
Iraqi Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz said on Sunday said his government had finalised a distribution plan but was awaiting a U.N. team to visit Baghdad to approve the plan.
Anbari acknowledged the delay in the resumption of crude sales meant Iraq would have to sell more oil between now and December, given current price levels, to meet the $2 billion ceiling.
But he said this would not be a problem.
"We have our capacity, both in terms of pipelines and production, of at least one million barrels per day and this could be increased easily," al-Anbari said.
"We can easily meet the ($2 billion) ceiling. We came up with this figure knowing our limitations and capacity."
To meet the target at current prices, oil sales starting in early August would require about a million bpd of Iraqi exports.
---Geneva Newsroom 41-22-733 38 31
